title: Shloka 109
subtitle: The thousand-petalled lotus, where every particular becomes all

namas.translation: Above the six wheels opens the lotus of a thousand petals, and there she takes her place.

compound.gloss: she who stands in the lotus of a thousand petals

namas.translation: All shades adorn her, and since varṇa also names a letter of the alphabet, the whole range of speech-sounds shines in her too.

compound.gloss: she who is made beautiful by all the colours

children.gloss: colour; also a letter of the alphabet

namas.translation: Whatever arms exist she holds, so that no instrument of protection is missing from her hands.
The bright constituent, the last and finest distillation of the bodily elements, is where she rests.

compound.gloss: she who is settled in the bright constituent

children.gloss: the bright or white substance; the generative fluid

namas.translation: There is no direction she does not look toward, and so no worshipper stands behind her back.

compound.gloss: she whose face is turned in every direction

children.gloss: from or in all directions, everywhere

commentary.meaning: For six stanzas the hymn has been climbing a ladder, one stanza for each wheel of the subtle body, and each built to the same specification: where she sits, what colour she is, how many faces she has, what she holds, which bodily constituent she occupies, what food pleases her, who attends her, and which of the Ḍākinī-goddesses she is. This verse begins the seventh and last of those stanzas, and it keeps the template while emptying every slot of its particulars. The seat is no longer one of the six wheels but the thousand-petalled lotus above them. The single colour becomes all colours. The count of faces, which had risen from one to six across the preceding stanzas, becomes a face turned in every direction at once. The named weapons become all weapons. Only śukla is still a specific term, and it is specific because it is the last of the seven bodily constituents and the series has nowhere further to go. What is being described is not another wheel but the exhaustion of the enumeration.
commentary.history:
The six wheels — mūlādhāra at the base, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata at the heart, viśuddhi at the throat, ājñā between the brows — are the standard furniture of the yoga of the subtle body as it is set out in tantric handbooks, and the sahasrāra is characteristically not counted among them. It is described as lying at or above the crown of the head, and the descriptive tradition, of which Pūrṇānanda's Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa is the best known representative, pictures it as a lotus hanging downward with its face turned toward the earth. Everything the hymn has said about the six wheels has been said of places inside the body; the seventh place is where that geography runs out. The order in which the sahasrāra is reached is worth noticing too. This hymn has been ascending, base to crown, which is the order of yoga; other treatments descend from the crown, which is the order of emanation.

Sarvavarṇopaśobhitā is the pivot of the verse, and it turns on a word that means two things at once. Varṇa is colour, and it is also a letter of the alphabet — the term Sanskrit grammar actually uses for a speech-sound. Read the first way, the name says that where each of the six goddesses had one colour (dark, red, yellow, white), she at the crown has all of them. Read the second way, it points at the thousand petals themselves. The descriptive literature explains the thousand as the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet, from a to kṣa, repeated twenty times over the petals, so that the lotus is a diagram of the entire stock of articulate sound. The fifty letters as a divine collective are the mātṛkā, the little mothers, and the doctrine that the phonemes are the substance from which the world is assembled is one of the load-bearing ideas of this literature. On that reading the name is not decorative at all: she is adorned by all the letters because the petals are the letters.

Sarvāyudhadharā works the same reversal on the armament. The preceding stanzas each hand their goddess a definite weapon and then hedge — the skull-topped staff and the rest, the thunderbolt and the rest, the trident and the rest, the goad and the rest, every one of them with the Sanskrit ādi trailing behind it. The list was already admitting that it was partial. Here the hedge is dropped and the whole arsenal is simply given at once.

Śuklasaṃsthitā belongs to a scheme the hymn has been running quietly underneath the visible one. Classical Indian medicine describes the body as a sequence of seven dhātus, tissues refined out of one another in order, ending in śukra, the generative fluid, which is the last and most concentrated distillation. The hymn's own series across the six preceding stanzas is skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow — six of the seven, in order, though it begins with skin where the medical texts begin with rasa, the nutrient fluid. The seventh place in the series falls here, and śukla is its name. Some read the word not as the tissue but in its plain adjectival sense of white or bright, and take the name to mean that she is established in pure light, which suits the crown; the two readings are not in competition, and commentators tend to keep both.

Sarvatomukhī has a long pedigree outside this hymn. The Puruṣasūkta's cosmic person has a thousand heads and a thousand eyes; the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad and the Bhagavadgītā both describe the one being as having hands, feet, eyes and faces on every side. The word is also used of fire, whose flames go outward in all directions, and it carries in ordinary Sanskrit the sense of complete or all-embracing. The devotional inference is drawn plainly by the tradition and needs no elaboration: if she faces every direction, no worshipper is ever standing behind her.
commentary.practice:
This verse and the one that follows it are usually chanted as a single unit, because the seventh cakra stanza does not finish until yākinyambāsvarūpiṇī. Reciters who stop at sarvatomukhī leave the description hanging without its goddess. In the sequential worship where each name is offered separately, the datives are sahasradalapadmasthāyai, sarvavarṇopaśobhitāyai, sarvāyudhadharāyai, śuklasaṃsthitāyai — the ordinary -āyai of feminine ā-stems — but sarvatomukhī is an ī-stem and gives sarvatomukhyai, with the ī contracting to y before the ending. That one break in the pattern is where the ending is most often got wrong.

The first line is hard for reasons of consonant clusters rather than length. Sahasradalapadmasthā has dma, a dental d released into a labial m, and then sthā, a dental s followed by an aspirated dental th. Neither will survive being hurried. Say pad-ma with the d actually pronounced and not assimilated into the m, and let sthā take its full aspiration. In the second name, varṇo has a retroflex ṇ — the tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth — and it is retroflex because of the r that precedes it, which is worth knowing because the same change will show up in svarūpiṇī in the next verse. The o of varṇo is a junction: varṇa plus upaśobhitā, a short a meeting a short u, which in Sanskrit gives o.

In the second line, śukla begins with the palatal ś, made further forward than English sh, and follows it with kla, which English speakers tend to break with a vowel. Keep it as one release. Saṃsthitā puts an anusvāra in front of the sth cluster: the nasal is held, then the cluster is articulated cleanly, saṃ-sthi-tā, three distinct beats. Sarvatomukhī ends on a long ī, and the final long vowel of a pāda tends to get clipped when a reciter is already thinking about the next line.

As to what the verse asks: it is the terminus of a practice that has been moving upward through the body, and the whole ascent is meant to be visualised in order, wheel by wheel, before the crown is reached. Practitioners who place the mantra on the body before recitation will have already touched these locations. The particular discipline of this stanza is that it withholds a fixed image. Every earlier station could be pictured — a colour, a face, a weapon in a hand. Here the colour is all colours, the faces are in every direction, the hands hold everything there is. There is nothing left that the visual imagination can pin down, and the tradition treats that failure of the image as the point rather than as a defect in the description.

crossReferences.deva: महीं मूलाधारे कमपि मणिपूरे हुतवहं स्थितं स्वाधिष्ठाने हृदि मरुतमाकाशमुपरि । मनोऽपि भ्रूमध्ये सकलमपि भित्त्वा कुलपथं सहस्रारे पद्मे सह रहसि पत्या विहरसे ॥
crossReferences.iast: mahīṃ mūlādhāre kamapi maṇipūre hutavahaṃ sthitaṃ svādhiṣṭhāne hṛdi marutam ākāśam upari | mano'pi bhrūmadhye sakalam api bhittvā kulapathaṃ sahasrāre padme saha rahasi patyā viharase ||
crossReferences.translation: Piercing earth in the root-support, water in the jewelled city, the fire that stands in her own place, wind at the heart, space above that, and mind between the brows — piercing the whole path of the family, you take your pleasure with your husband in the thousand-petalled lotus, alone.
crossReferences.relevance: The classic statement of the ascent that this stanza completes, and the reason the crown is where the hymn's series ends. Note that the poem puts water in maṇipūra and fire in svādhiṣṭhāna, the reverse of the assignment most later handbooks give; the commentators know this and argue about it, and the disagreement is a useful reminder that the subtle body was described differently by different schools.

crossReferences.deva: सर्वतःपाणिपादं तत् सर्वतोऽक्षिशिरोमुखम् । सर्वतःश्रुतिमल्लोके सर्वमावृत्य तिष्ठति ॥
crossReferences.iast: sarvataḥpāṇipādaṃ tat sarvato'kṣiśiromukham | sarvataḥśrutimal loke sarvam āvṛtya tiṣṭhati ||
crossReferences.translation: With hands and feet on every side, with eyes and heads and faces on every side, with hearing on every side, it stands in the world, having covered everything.
crossReferences.relevance: Sarvatomukhī is not an invention of this hymn but the reuse of a formula that Vedānta had long applied to the one being, and which the Gītā and the Śvetāśvatara share word for word. Reading it here shows what the hymn is doing when it stops counting faces: it drops out of the language of iconography, where a figure has a definite number of heads, and into the language of the Upaniṣads, where facing every direction is a way of saying that nothing is outside.

references.title: The Serpent Power: The Secrets of Tantric and Shaktic Yoga
references.author: Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe)
references.note: Dated in its framing and unreliable when it philosophises, but it contains a full translation of Pūrṇānanda's Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, which is the text that actually describes the seven lotuses petal by petal with their letters. Read the translated verses and the Sanskrit, and treat the long introduction as a period piece.

references.title: Kuṇḍalinī: The Energy of the Depths
references.author: Lilian Silburn, tr. Jacques Gontier (SUNY Press, 1988)
references.note: A far more careful account of the subtle body than Woodroffe's, drawn from the Kashmirian sources. Useful here because Silburn is precise about what the sahasrāra is and is not: not a seventh wheel in the same series as the six, but the place where the series terminates.

references.title: The Roots of Ayurveda: Selections from Sanskrit Medical Writings
references.author: Dominik Wujastyk (Penguin Classics, revised ed. 2003)
references.note: The quickest way to see what the seven dhātus are in the tradition that invented them, with translated passages from Caraka and Suśruta. Without this background śuklasaṃsthitā and the six tissue-names in the preceding stanzas look arbitrary; with it they are a complete and ordered list.

references.title: Lalitā Sahasranāma with Bhāskararāya's Commentary (Saubhāgyabhāskara)
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Theosophical Publishing House, Adyar)
references.note: The standard English window onto the commentary that most later expositions depend on. It is worth consulting on this verse specifically to see how much of the tradition's reading of the cakra stanzas is scriptural citation rather than free interpretation — Bhāskararāya argues, he does not simply assert.

references.title: A Sanskrit–English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Look up varṇa and śukla here before accepting any single translation of this verse. Varṇa gives colour, letter, class and quality in one entry, and śukla gives white, bright and the generative fluid, which is precisely the ambiguity the commentators are working with.
